frame-u01.name: KP05 Sparse connectivity and parameter sharing
frame-u01.text: KP05 Sparse connectivity and parameter sharing

scene-u01-pnew1-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew1-26.text: KP04 ended: the same multiply-and-add can also be written as one huge fully connected layer.

scene-u01-pnew1-28.name: text#28
scene-u01-pnew1-28.text:
convolutional layer
(a small kernel slides and multiplies-adds)

scene-u01-pnew1-30.name: text#30
scene-u01-pnew1-30.text:
fully connected layer
(weight matrix times input)

scene-u01-pnew1-65.name: text#65
scene-u01-pnew1-65.text: Compared with a fully connected layer, what does convolution save?

scene-u01-pnew1-70.name: text#70
scene-u01-pnew1-70.text: There are three things that can be saved: weights, connections, multiply-adds.

scene-u01-pnew2-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew2-25.text: Convolution as a matrix: zeros are sparsity, repeated numbers are sharing

scene-u01-pnew2-109.name: text#109
scene-u01-pnew2-109.text:
zeros: each output sees only $3$ cells
→ sparse connectivity

scene-u01-pnew2-111.name: text#111
scene-u01-pnew2-111.text:
each row is the same $1,2,-1$ moved right
→ parameter sharing

scene-u01-pnew2-145.name: text#145
scene-u01-pnew2-145.text: A convolutional layer is a fully connected layer whose matrix is mostly 0 with repeated rows.

scene-u01-pnew3-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew3-25.text: Before comparing, separate the three things to count

scene-u01-pnew3-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew3-26.text: They are not the same number: weights, connections, multiply-adds.

scene-u01-pnew3-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew3-37.text:
how many different learnable numbers
(stored by the model, learned from data)

scene-u01-pnew3-52.name: text#52
scene-u01-pnew3-52.text:
how many paths from an input into an output
(the non-zero cells of the matrix)

scene-u01-pnew3-60.name: text#60
scene-u01-pnew3-60.text:
how many times we multiply by a weight and add into a sum
one per connection, so multiply-adds = connections

scene-u01-pnew3-62.name: text#62
scene-u01-pnew3-62.text: Weights are how much to remember; connections and multiply-adds are how much to compute.

scene-u01-pnew4-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew4-25.text: The three layers: the same 6 inputs and 4 outputs

scene-u01-pnew4-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew4-26.text: One line is one connection; lines of the same colour share one weight.

scene-u01-pnew4-115.name: text#115
scene-u01-pnew4-115.text: Connections $24\to12\to12$: sparsity cuts connections; sharing only lets same-coloured lines share a number.

scene-u01-pnew5-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew5-25.text: What each restriction saves: sparsity $M/k$ times, sharing $P$ times

scene-u01-pnew5-46.name: text#46
scene-u01-pnew5-46.text: The two factors multiply: $2\times4=8=\dfrac{MP}{k}=\dfrac{24}{3}$, the total shrink of the weights.

scene-u01-pnew5-48.name: text#48
scene-u01-pnew5-48.text: Only sparsity saves connections and multiply-adds; sharing saves weights.

scene-u01-pnew6-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew6-25.text: Common error: believing "sharing makes the computation smaller"

scene-u01-pnew6-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew6-26.text: Put weights and multiply-adds side by side and see which one drops.

scene-u01-pnew6-84.name: text#84
scene-u01-pnew6-84.text: Every output still does its own $k$ multiply-adds; it is sparsity that saves them.

scene-u01-pnew7-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew7-25.text: On a larger image the gap grows: a $28\times28$ image with one $5\times5$ kernel

scene-u01-pnew7-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew7-26.text: Valid output $24\times24$, so $M=784$, $P=576$, $k=25$ (one kernel, biases excluded).

scene-u01-pnew7-115.name: text#115
scene-u01-pnew7-115.text: Weights fall $18{,}063.36$ times; multiply-adds only from $451{,}584$ to $14{,}400$ (about $31$ times).

scene-u01-pnew8-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew8-25.text: What if the window grows? Fix $M=6$ and let $k$ go from $1$ to $6$

scene-u01-pnew8-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew8-26.text: The number of outputs is $P=7-k$; the weights of the three layers change with $k$.

scene-u01-pnew8-87.name: text#87
scene-u01-pnew8-87.text: When the window is as large as the input, the three layers have the same number of weights.

scene-u01-pnew9-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew9-25.text: Why do they meet? As the window grows, both savings shrink to $1$

scene-u01-pnew9-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew9-26.text: Sparsity saves $M/k$ times; sharing saves $P=M-k+1$ times (the number of positions the window fits).

scene-u01-pnew9-45.name: text#45
scene-u01-pnew9-45.text:
sparsity saves $M/k=2$ times
sharing saves $P=4$ times

scene-u01-pnew9-64.name: text#64
scene-u01-pnew9-64.text:
sparsity saves $M/k=1.2$ times
sharing saves $P=2$ times

scene-u01-pnew9-82.name: text#82
scene-u01-pnew9-82.text:
sparsity saves $M/k=1$ times
sharing saves $P=1$ times

scene-u01-pnew9-88.name: text#88
scene-u01-pnew9-88.text: $k=M$: one position only; no connections to cut and no other position to share with.

scene-u01-pnew10-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew10-26.text: Sparse alone is a locally connected layer; sharing alone is meaningless.

scene-u01-pnew10-65.name: text#65
scene-u01-pnew10-65.text: each position learns its own $k$ weights: $kP=12$

scene-u01-pnew10-118.name: text#118
scene-u01-pnew10-118.text:
✗ sharing without sparsity?
needs a window smaller than the input

scene-u01-pnew10-120.name: text#120
scene-u01-pnew10-120.text:
window = input: one position,
nothing to share

scene-u01-pnew10-126.name: text#126
scene-u01-pnew10-126.text: A small window (sparsity) comes first; only then does sharing make sense.

scene-u01-pnew11-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew11-25.text: The two restrictions are two assumptions: when do they fail?

scene-u01-pnew11-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew11-26.text: They are built into the model before it sees any data (inductive bias).

scene-u01-pnew11-28.name: text#28
scene-u01-pnew11-28.text:
assumption 1: patterns are local
→ sparse connectivity

scene-u01-pnew11-32.name: text#32
scene-u01-pnew11-32.text:
edges and textures need only nearby cells,
a small patch is enough

scene-u01-pnew11-34.name: text#34
scene-u01-pnew11-34.text:
assumption 2: same pattern, same meaning
→ parameter sharing

scene-u01-pnew11-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew11-38.text: a cat's ear in the upper left or the lower right is still a cat's ear

scene-u01-pnew11-40.name: text#40
scene-u01-pnew11-40.text: when it fails: position carries meaning

scene-u01-pnew11-45.name: text#45
scene-u01-pnew11-45.text:
e.g. aligned faces, eyes always at the same place
→ consider a locally connected layer ($P$ times more weights)

scene-u01-pnew11-47.name: text#47
scene-u01-pnew11-47.text: When the assumption holds the restriction is a gain; when it fails it hurts.

scene-u01-pnew12-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew12-25.text: A benefit of sharing: one weight sees many examples

scene-u01-pnew12-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew12-26.text: In backpropagation a shared weight receives the gradients of all $P$ positions, added up.

scene-u01-pnew12-43.name: text#43
scene-u01-pnew12-43.text: every position throws in a share of gradient

scene-u01-pnew12-67.name: text#67
scene-u01-pnew12-67.text: summed up, I learn more steadily!

scene-u01-pnew12-69.name: text#69
scene-u01-pnew12-69.text: Each shared weight is "taught" by $P$ positions at every step.

scene-u01-pnew13-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew13-25.text: Summary: a convolutional layer is a fully connected layer with two restrictions

scene-u01-pnew13-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew13-26.text: Count three things separately: weights, connections, multiply-adds.

scene-u01-pnew13-36.name: text#36
scene-u01-pnew13-36.text: sparsity: weights, connections, multiply-adds all save $M/k$

scene-u01-pnew13-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew13-38.text: sharing: only weights save a further $P$

scene-u01-pnew13-40.name: text#40
scene-u01-pnew13-40.text: At $k=M$ the three layers coincide; when position matters, sharing may not fit.

scene-u01-pnew13-62.name: text#62
scene-u01-pnew13-62.text:
next: KP06 translation equivariance
the output follows the pattern

scene-u01-pnew13-64.name: text#64
scene-u01-pnew13-64.text: Sparsity saves connections and multiply-adds, sharing saves weights; together they make the layer light.

steps.label: KP05 Sparse connectivity and parameter sharing
KP05 · 1/13
steps.speakerNotes: KP04 ended by noting that the same sliding multiply-and-add can also be written as one huge fully connected layer.

steps.label: KP05 · 1/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: KP04 ended by noting that the same sliding multiply-and-add can also be written as one huge fully connected layer.

steps.label: KP05 · 1/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: So the question: compared with a fully connected layer, what does convolution save? The little model wants to know too.

steps.label: KP05 · 1/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: There is more than one answer: weights, connections and multiply-adds are three different things. We separate them first, then see which one each restriction saves.

steps.label: KP05 · 2/13
steps.speakerNotes: The input x has six cells and the kernel w is 1, 2, minus 1. Look at the weight matrix first: row 0 holds the three numbers of the kernel in its first three cells and zeros elsewhere.

steps.label: KP05 · 2/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The input x has six cells and the kernel w is 1, 2, minus 1. Look at the weight matrix first: row 0 holds the three numbers of the kernel in its first three cells and zeros elsewhere.

steps.label: KP05 · 2/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Moving the same numbers one cell right in every row fills the four rows. A zero means the connection does not exist, which is sparse connectivity; the repeated three numbers mean all outputs use the same kernel, which is parameter sharing.

steps.label: KP05 · 2/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The matrix times the input gives four outputs: 1, 7, 2, minus 2. For example the first output is 2 times 1, plus 1 times 2, plus 3 times minus 1, which is 1. So a convolutional layer is a special fully connected layer.

steps.label: KP05 · 3/13
steps.speakerNotes: First: weights, the number of different learnable numbers, that is what the model must store and learn from data.

steps.label: KP05 · 3/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: First: weights, the number of different learnable numbers, that is what the model must store and learn from data.

steps.label: KP05 · 3/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Second: connections, the number of paths from an input into an output, that is the non-zero cells of the weight matrix.

steps.label: KP05 · 3/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Third: multiply-adds, how many times we multiply by a weight and add into a sum to compute all outputs. One per connection, so multiply-adds equal connections. Weights are how much to remember; connections and multiply-adds are how much to compute.

steps.label: KP05 · 4/13
steps.speakerNotes: The same six inputs and four outputs. In the fully connected layer every output connects to all six inputs: twenty-four grey lines, each an independent weight.

steps.label: KP05 · 4/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The same six inputs and four outputs. In the fully connected layer every output connects to all six inputs: twenty-four grey lines, each an independent weight.

steps.label: KP05 · 4/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Sparse but not shared: each output connects to only three inputs, leaving twelve lines, each still with its own colour, so twelve different weights.

steps.label: KP05 · 4/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Sparse and shared, the convolutional layer: still twelve lines, but only three colours, lines of one colour use the same weight, so three weights. Connections go 24, 12, 12; sharing does not remove connections.

steps.label: KP05 · 5/13
steps.speakerNotes: Top row: weights. The fully connected layer has twenty-four. Adding sparsity, each output sees three cells, down to twelve, a saving of M over k, two times; adding sharing, four outputs share one set, down to three, a saving of P, four times.

steps.label: KP05 · 5/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Top row: weights. The fully connected layer has twenty-four. Adding sparsity, each output sees three cells, down to twelve, a saving of M over k, two times; adding sharing, four outputs share one set, down to three, a saving of P, four times.

steps.label: KP05 · 5/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Bottom row: connections and multiply-adds. Sparsity also takes them from twenty-four to twelve; but sharing removes no connection, they stay twelve.

steps.label: KP05 · 5/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The two factors multiply: two times four is eight, exactly the total shrink of the weights, twenty-four to three. Only sparsity saves connections and multiply-adds; sharing saves weights.

steps.label: KP05 · 6/13
steps.speakerNotes: Put weights and multiply-adds side by side. Red is weights: twenty-four, twelve, three.

steps.label: KP05 · 6/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Put weights and multiply-adds side by side. Red is weights: twenty-four, twelve, three.

steps.label: KP05 · 6/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Green is multiply-adds: twenty-four, twelve, twelve. The convolutional layer's weights fall to three, but its multiply-adds stay twelve.

steps.label: KP05 · 6/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: So "sharing makes the computation smaller" is wrong. Every output still does its own k multiply-adds, because every position still gets one look. Sparsity saves multiply-adds; sharing saves weights.

steps.label: KP05 · 7/13
steps.speakerNotes: Now an image: a twenty-eight by twenty-eight grayscale image with one five by five kernel; the valid output is twenty-four by twenty-four, so M is 784, P is 576 and k is 25.

steps.label: KP05 · 7/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Now an image: a twenty-eight by twenty-eight grayscale image with one five by five kernel; the valid output is twenty-four by twenty-four, so M is 784, P is 576 and k is 25.

steps.label: KP05 · 7/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The weights of the three layers: 451,584 for the fully connected layer; 14,400 sparse but not shared; only 25 with sharing. The bar lengths are on a log scale, only a sketch.

steps.label: KP05 · 7/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Sparsity saves M over k, 31.36 times; sharing saves P, 576 times; together 18,063.36 times. But the multiply-adds fall only from 451,584 to 14,400, about 31 times.

steps.label: KP05 · 8/13
steps.speakerNotes: Fix M at six and let the window k go from one to six. The red line is the fully connected layer, falling from thirty-six to six, because there are fewer and fewer outputs.

steps.label: KP05 · 8/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Fix M at six and let the window k go from one to six. The red line is the fully connected layer, falling from thirty-six to six, because there are fewer and fewer outputs.

steps.label: KP05 · 8/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The orange line is sparse but not shared; it rises and then falls: six, ten, twelve, twelve, ten, six.

steps.label: KP05 · 8/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The green line is sparse and shared; its weights are k, rising from one to six. At the far right, where k equals M, the three lines meet at one point, all six.

steps.label: KP05 · 9/13
steps.speakerNotes: Look at one row: window k equals three, the window fits in four positions. Sparsity saves M over k, two times; sharing saves P, four times, eight times together.

steps.label: KP05 · 9/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Look at one row: window k equals three, the window fits in four positions. Sparsity saves M over k, two times; sharing saves P, four times, eight times together.

steps.label: KP05 · 9/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: With k equal to five only two positions remain: sparsity saves just 1.2 times and sharing only two times.

steps.label: KP05 · 9/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: With k equal to M, six: only one position remains. The window already sees the whole input, so there is no connection to cut, and with one position there is no other position to share with. Both factors are one and the three layers become the same.

steps.label: KP05 · 10/13
steps.speakerNotes: Sparse without sharing is called a locally connected layer: every position learns its own k weights, so there are k times P, here twelve.

steps.label: KP05 · 10/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Sparse without sharing is called a locally connected layer: every position learns its own k weights, so there are k times P, here twelve.

steps.label: KP05 · 10/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Add sharing and the same k weights are used at every position: that is the convolutional layer, with only three. In the image example the locally connected layer has over fourteen thousand, 576 times the twenty-five of the convolutional layer.

steps.label: KP05 · 10/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Sharing without sparsity is meaningless: to use the same weights at different positions we first need a window smaller than the input. When the window is as large as the input there is one position and nothing to share.

steps.label: KP05 · 11/13
steps.speakerNotes: The two restrictions are really two assumptions about the data. First: useful patterns are local, so an output needs only a small nearby patch. Edges and textures in photographs are like that.

steps.label: KP05 · 11/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The two restrictions are really two assumptions about the data. First: useful patterns are local, so an output needs only a small nearby patch. Edges and textures in photographs are like that.

steps.label: KP05 · 11/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Second: the same pattern means the same wherever it appears. A cat's ear in the upper left or the lower right is still a cat's ear, so one kernel can serve both.

steps.label: KP05 · 11/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: When an assumption fails, the restriction hurts. If position itself carries meaning in the task, for example aligned faces with the eyes always in the same place, sharing forces different positions to use one kernel, which does not fit; a locally connected layer can be considered, at the cost of P times more weights. This is an example, not a rule.

steps.label: KP05 · 12/13
steps.speakerNotes: Sharing has a consequence in backpropagation. One weight w[m] of the kernel is used at all P positions, so its gradient is the sum of the contributions of all P positions.

steps.label: KP05 · 12/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Sharing has a consequence in backpropagation. One weight w[m] of the kernel is used at all P positions, so its gradient is the sum of the contributions of all P positions.

steps.label: KP05 · 12/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: In the figure, four positions each throw in a share of gradient into the same shared weight.

steps.label: KP05 · 12/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Every shared weight therefore sees many examples and is learned more steadily. This is another benefit of sharing, beyond saving weights.

steps.label: KP05 · 13/13
steps.speakerNotes: Summary: a convolutional layer is a fully connected layer with two restrictions. Sparse connectivity: each output sees only k cells; parameter sharing: one kernel over the whole image.

steps.label: KP05 · 13/13 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Summary: a convolutional layer is a fully connected layer with two restrictions. Sparse connectivity: each output sees only k cells; parameter sharing: one kernel over the whole image.

steps.label: KP05 · 13/13 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Sparsity saves weights, connections and multiply-adds by M over k; sharing saves only weights, by a further P. At k equal to M the three layers coincide; when position matters, sharing may not fit.

steps.label: KP05 · 13/13 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Next, KP06: wherever a pattern moves, the output moves with it, called translation equivariance. Sparsity saves connections and multiply-adds, sharing saves weights; together they make the layer light.
